title: Kubernetes Explained in 6 Minutes _ k8s Architecture

segments.text: Why this Kubernetes? Why is it called KAS? What makes it so popular? Let's take a look.
Kubernetes is an open source container orchestration platform. It all amazed the deployment,
scaling, and management of containerized applications. Kubernetes can be traced back to
Google's internal container orchestration system board, which managed the deployment of
thousands of applications within Google. In 2014, Google opens source a version of
work that is Kubernetes. Now, why is it called KAS? This is a somewhat nerdy way of
abbreviating long words. The number 8 in KAS referred to the 8 letters between the
first letter K and the last letter S in the work Kubernetes. Other examples that I18 and
for internationalization and L10 and for localization. A Kubernetes cluster is a set of
machines called notes that are used to run containerized applications. There are two core pieces
in a Kubernetes cluster. The first is the control plane. This responsible for managing
the state of the cluster. In production environments, the control plane usually runs on multiple
notes that span across several data centers zones. The second is the set of worker notes.
These notes run the containerized application workloads. The containerized applications run
in a pot. Pot are the smallest deployable units in Kubernetes. Pot hosts one or more containers
and provides share storage and networking for those containers. Pot's are created and managed by
Kubernetes control plane. They are the basic building blocks of Kubernetes applications.
Now, let's dive a bit deeper into the control plane. You consist of a number of core components.
They are the API server, SCD, scheduler, and the controller manager. The API server is the primary
interface between the control plane and the rest of the cluster. It exposes a
restful API that allows clients to interact with the control plane and submit requests to
manage the cluster. SCD is a distributed key value store. It stores the clusters for
system state. This used by the API server and other components of the control plane to
store and retrieve information about the cluster. The scheduler is responsible for scheduling
parts onto the worker notes in the cluster. It uses information about the resources we
acquire by the parts and available resources on the worker notes to make placement decisions.
The controller manager is responsible for running controllers that manage the
state of the cluster. Some examples include a replication controller, which ensures that
the desired number of replicas of a part running and the deployment controller, which
manages the rolling updates and rollbacks of deployments. Next, let's dive deeper into the
worker notes. The core components of Kubernetes that run on the worker notes include
Kubernetes, container runtime, and coop proxy. The Kubernetes is a demand that runs on each
worker note. This responsible for communicating with the control plane. It receives
instruction from the control plane about which parts to run on the note and ensures that the
desired state of the parts is maintained. The container runtime runs the containers on the
note. It is responsible for pulling the container images from the registry, starting and
stopping the containers, and managing the containers resources. The coop proxy is a
networking proxy that runs on each worker note. It is responsible for routing traffic
to the correct parts. It also provides low balancing for the parts and ensures that the
traffic is distributed evenly across the parts. So why should we use Kubernetes as
with many things in software engineering? This is all about trade-offs. Let's look at the
upsize first. Kubernetes is scalable and highly available. It provides features like self-healing,
automatic, rollbacks, and horizontal scaling. It makes it easy to scale our application up and
down as needed, allowing us to respond to changes in demand quickly. Kubernetes is portable.
It helps us deploy and manage applications in a consistent and reliable way regardless of the
underlying infrastructure. It runs on premise, in a public cloud, or in a hybrid environment. It
provides a uniform way to package, deploy, and manage applications. Now, how about the downsides?
The number one drawback is complexity. Kubernetes is complex to set up and operate. The
upfront class is high, especially for organizations new to container orchestration. It requires a
high level of expertise and resources to set up and manage a production Kubernetes environment.
The second drawback is cost. Kubernetes requires a certain minimum level of resources to run
in order to support all the features we mentioned about. It's likely an overkill for many smaller
organizations. One popular option that strikes a reasonable balance is to offload the
management of the control plane to a managed Kubernetes service. Management Kubernetes services
are provided by cloud providers. Some popular ones are Amazon, EKS, GKE, and Google Cloud,
and AKS on Azure. These services allow organizations to run Kubernetes applications
without having to worry about the underlying infrastructure. They take care of tasks that we
acquired deep expertise by setting up and configuring the control plane, scaling the cluster,
and providing ongoing maintenance and support. This is a reasonable option for a mid-sized
organization to test our Kubernetes. For a smaller organization, Yankney is our recommendation.
If you would like to learn more about system design, check out books and weekly newsletter.
Please subscribe if you learned something new. Thank you so much and we'll see you next time.
